title: In the Place of My Ashes
subtitle: As day breaks, the story ends where the ashes rest. In the end, the night is not eternal.

trails.title: A Secret Meeting
trails.description: In 1991, information moved at lightning speed thanks to technological advancement!

content.text: The moment armies start to march, the world stands still.
You fight or fall back, charge forward, or run. Those are the only rules on the battlefield.
I don't see a start time on this report, nor does it state the reason for or the demands of this war.
That's because the war hasn't started yet.

branch.text: That's what you think. The scars left on the land may be the most obvious form of destruction, but the true devastation of war is one that develops gradually in the souls of people.
Ah, a literary war. Indeed, the violence enacted upon words is often just as devastating as an order on a battlefield.
Words must fulfill their duties to their creators, just as soldiers must answer to their commanders.
I still don't see how this relates to what's happening now.
You don't? Hmm. The young writers have been exiled—sent down a path with no signs to follow and no destination.
In dark days of bloody conflict, soldiers often find comfort in scriptures and verses—or in letters from their loved ones.
They hold those words close—a fragile piece of home—a brief solace from the roaring of the battlefield.
But, as they fall one by one, they learn the bitter truth. No destiny awaits them but death, that bitter homesickness still weighing heavy in their hearts.
I hope they can at least find some peace in their dreams.
In dreams? Maybe. Walking the streets of your hometown, spending a lazy afternoon at the writing desk—dreams can take you anywhere.
But live there too long, and the lines between fiction and reality will blur, and soon you'll never wake up again.
Soldiers crawl through trenches, roll in the mud, and charge to their deaths again and again ...
... while words are forever trapped within the confines of poetry, made to live, die, and live again under the golden prophecy ...
Ugh. I can't stand the way poets talk.

content.text: Because this is a war waged with paper and pens.

items.text: In the Place of My Ashes
Blazing flames reflect in their eyes, just like the name of this island might suggest.
A winter night stands sentinel over a great conflagration as every brick of Comala Prison crumbles and falls.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: With Aleph's control gone, Comala is collapsing.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: The inmates aren't even real criminals, are they? And they're still in there, with no clue that they're no longer being watched from the central tower!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: We have to go tell them! We have to get them to safety!

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Yes, we should help them get out, at least until support arrives.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: But the Manus ritual ...
The battered boat sways within their sight.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Don't worry. I'll go alone.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Huh?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: You should hurry. When this is all over, I'll write to you, my dear friend!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: During this journey together, our teamwork has been impeccable. So, you can trust me to do this.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I'm not doing it just to help you or the organization you represent. I'm doing it because the inmates are my friends.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Okay. I trust you.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Take care of yourself, Recoleta.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: But if the "Storm" truly is imminent, as Dr. Merlin said, then, Ms. Recoleta, you'll ...

Sonetto, more familiar than anyone with the Foundation's exhaustive regulations, has no ready answer. She knows that, in this era, before those arcanists who remain ignorant of the truth, she must watch her words.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I don't quite understand what this "Storm" is all about, but don't worry. A brand-new adventure is the best thing that can happen to a writer.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: And I doubt it'll surpass the epic adventures we've shared over the past couple of days. I'm going to write everything, including the two of you, into my new novel.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Then I'd like to be the first to read this new novel, if that's alright?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Of course. Listen, I believe literature is like an endless, timeless river.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: So we'll meet again someday, somewhere, probably in someone else's story. Who knows?
She takes one last look at her new friends, feeling a longing as if they had known each other for decades.
Then, without a backward glance, the girl sprints back to the burning ruins of the prison.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Farewell, my cherished friends!
I hear a sound in the distance
Guiding me on to a land of existence
So I journey on to a path that feels real
There is a voice that's calling me
To somewhere far—
Have mercy, please!
For happiness, I sing to you
And for freedom, I sing to you
Nothing can break me, nothing bring me down
Like a child I leap around
For happiness, I sing to you ...
All the visitors depart one after another.
Amid the distant echo of singing, the "creator" of this prison stares into the fire as it burns.
The moment holds for a time, until a breathless jaguar appears at the dock's edge, staring at the human before her with uncertainty.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Dr. Merlin. You're Dr. Merlin, right? I finally found you.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: What on earth happened in the central tower? Right after I left, the whole Panopticon started collapsing. The tower's in ruin.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I've been looking for you everywhere. Please, sir, come with me. It isn't saf—

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: That won't be necessary.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: The snow is still falling, yet everything in the labyrinth has already gone up in flames.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: Fortune, fate, karma—They're nothing but a ridiculous joke.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: It's over, jaguar. You have lost your memories, your identity, your name, and now, your title. You are no longer a jailer trapped in the Panopticon.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I don't get it, Dr. Merlin. What are you talking about?
The jailer takes a step back, her predator instincts sensing the danger in the words to come.
The damage may not be physical, but it threatens to shatter what little faith she has left to hold onto, and the life she has always known.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I'm-I'm going back to Comala. Order must be maintained. The prisoners mustn't be allowed to escape.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Please take care, Dr. Merlin.
Nerves torn between panic and hesitation, the jailer at last turns toward the searing flames.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Hey, you! Don't run off like that. It's dangerous!
No one heeds her cries.
One prisoner after another flees in terror, escaping the crumbling labyrinth.

items.speaker: Inmate I
items.text: In deserts, in stars, in labyrinths!

items.speaker: Inmate II
items.text: We dream on death's straw pillow!
The jailer drifts through the raging scene, unable to steer a sensible course. At last, she pins down a frail and powerless prisoner beneath her weight.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Stop!
Get off me! Let me go!
Are you blind? The Panopticon is falling apart!

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: It's you, Roberta.
The jailer recognizes the prisoner under her grip.
Roberta, a kind and quiet prisoner, always well-behaved, now panicked and desperate to escape.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: They're all mad! I knew it. They've been insane from the start!

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: The whole place is burning to the ground, and they still won't leave! They're still talking and talking about things that no one cares about.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: Ah! I can't help them. I've never understood what they were talking about—the rhythms, the factions, the ideologies ...

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: Yes, the people were nice, the Idealist, too, but I've had enough of this prison. I've had enough of the Panopticon.
She collapses onto the ground, sobbing.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: I never should've joined these movements. It was all meaningless from the beginning.

items.speaker: Roberta
items.text: I wanna leave this place—go to Spain or France, anywhere but here. I want to go back to Magdalena.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Huh ...
The jaguar releases her grip. Without a backward glance, Roberta leaves.
The jailer steps back into the circular structure she knows as her only home.
For happiness, I sing to you
And for freedom, I sing to you
Nothing can break me, nothing bring me down
Under the night sky, she sees Comala Prison glowing like a brilliant bonfire.
Street, Ushuaia
Three days ago

items.speaker: Dores
items.text: But how does literature make you feel?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: As though I'm a kid looking through a kaleidoscope for the first time.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Well, maybe that's not the best way to put it. Perhaps something a little more subtle.
The young writer drowns in the vortex of words as the blind woman walks away.
She walks silently toward Comala Prison, arriving at the dock hidden between cliffs and reefs.
There, the prisoner who answers all questions awaits her arrival.

items.speaker: Dores
items.text: A ship sailing to an unfamiliar land.

items.speaker: Dores
items.text: A parable of the past and future. An era that once existed and is yet to come.

items.speaker: Dores
items.text: Is this the answer you've provided, Mr. Aleph?

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: No, Urd. You will have to find this answer yourself.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: No one can help you with this—no one.

items.speaker: Dores
items.text: I see. Thank you, Mr. Aleph. I will remember what you've told me.
So the platonic year
Whirls out new right and wrong,
Whirls in the old instead;
All men are dancers and their tread
Goes to the barbarous clangour of a gong.
W.B. Yeats—Nineteen Hundred and Nineteen
